function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

context_from.description: Optional job ID or list of job IDs whose most recent completed output is injected into the prompt as context before each run. Use this to chain cron jobs: job A collects data, job B processes it. Each entry must be a valid job ID (from cronjob action='list'). Note: injects the most recent completed output — does not wait for upstream jobs running in the same tick. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

enabled_toolsets.description: Optional list of toolset names to restrict the job's agent to (e.g. ["web", "terminal", "file", "delegation"]). When set, only tools from these toolsets are loaded, significantly reducing input token overhead. When omitted, all default tools are loaded. Infer from the job's prompt — e.g. use "web" if it calls web_search, "terminal" if it runs scripts, "file" if it reads files, "delegation" if it calls delegate_task. On update, pass an empty array to clear.

workdir.description: Optional absolute path to run the job from. When set, AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from that directory are injected into the system prompt, and the terminal/file/code_exec tools use it as their working directory — useful for running a job inside a specific project repo. Must be an absolute path that exists. When unset (default), preserves the original behaviour: no project context files, tools use the scheduler's cwd. On update, pass an empty string to clear. Jobs with workdir run sequentially (not parallel) to keep per-job directories isolated.

function.name: session_search
function.description:
Search your long-term memory of past conversations, or browse recent sessions. This is your recall -- every past session is searchable, and this tool summarizes what happened.

TWO MODES:
1. Recent sessions (no query): Call with no arguments to see what was worked on recently. Returns titles, previews, and timestamps. Zero LLM cost, instant. Start here when the user asks what were we working on or what did we do recently.
2. Keyword search (with query): Search for specific topics across all past sessions. Returns LLM-generated summaries of matching sessions.

USE THIS PROACTIVELY when:
- The user says 'we did this before', 'remember when', 'last time', 'as I mentioned'
- The user asks about a topic you worked on before but don't have in current context
- The user references a project, person, or concept that seems familiar but isn't in memory
- You want to check if you've solved a similar problem before
- The user asks 'what did we do about X?' or 'how did we fix Y?'

Don't hesitate to search when it is actually cross-session -- it's fast and cheap. Better to search and confirm than to guess or ask the user to repeat themselves.

Search syntax: keywords joined with OR for broad recall (elevenlabs OR baseten OR funding), phrases for exact match ("docker networking"), boolean (python NOT java), prefix (deploy*). IMPORTANT: Use OR between keywords for best results — FTS5 defaults to AND which misses sessions that only mention some terms. If a broad OR query returns nothing, try individual keyword searches in parallel. Returns summaries of the top matching sessions.

query.description: Search query — keywords, phrases, or boolean expressions to find in past sessions. Omit this parameter entirely to browse recent sessions instead (returns titles, previews, timestamps with no LLM cost).

role_filter.description: Optional: only search messages from specific roles (comma-separated). E.g. 'user,assistant' to skip tool outputs.

function.description:

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

file_path.description: Path to a supporting file within the skill directory. For 'write_file'/'remove_file': required, must be under references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/. For 'patch': optional, defaults to SKILL.md if omitted.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

   361|
   362|### Engineering
   363|
   364|The company was everything Bob had hoped for and nothing like Fermilab. Where the lab had been academic, collaborative, focused on basic research, the aerospace contractor was competitive, classified, driven by schedules and deliverables and the absolute requirement that systems work perfectly every time.
   365|
   366|Bob's first assignment was avionics integration—combining navigation, communication, and flight control systems into coherent wholes that pilots could actually use. The work was challenging, the learning curve steep. He spent months studying aerodynamics, flight mechanics, human factors engineering—fields he had never encountered in his particle accelerator work. His colleagues were different too. Many were veterans, former pilots or Air Force engineers who spoke a language of sorties and flight envelopes and g-forces that Bob had to learn quickly. They were skeptical of the civilian from the physics lab, testing him with questions and challenges that bordered on hazing. Bob answered by working harder than anyone else. He studied flight manuals the way he had once studied physics textbooks, learned to speak the language, demonstrated through competence what he couldn't establish through credentials. Slowly, the veterans accepted him. Eventually, they respected him.
   367|
   368|Eventually , he was entrusted with more responsibility, working directly with test pilots to understand how systems performed in actual flight. He would analyze data from test runs, identify anomalies, suggest modifications, then watch as pilots took the aircraft up again to validate his recommendations. The work was intoxicating. Every flight generated new data, new insights, new problems to solve. Unlike the particle accelerator, which had operated within fixed parameters for years, the planes were constantly evolving, constantly pushing into fresh territory. Bob felt the excitement he had missed at Fermilab—the sense of being on a frontier.
   369|
   370|Bob earned his opportunity to join the flight test program at Eglin Air Force Base. It was the role he had imagined when he left Fermilab—the chance to work directly with aircraft, to understand their behavior through actual flight rather than simulation, to contribute to systems that would keep pilots safe at the edges of performance.
   371|
   372|Flight testing was engineering at its most demanding. Every mission generated immense amount of data—telemetry from hundreds of sensors, pilot reports, video recordings, environmental conditions. Bob's job was to analyze this data, find issues, recommend solutions, then confirm those solutions in later flights.
   373|
   374|He learned to read the sky, to understand weather as a variable in system performance. He learned the physiology of flight—how g-forces affected pilot capability, how altitude changed system behavior, how the human-machine interface broke down under stress. He spent hours in briefings and debriefings with pilots, developing the trust necessary for honest communication about what worked and what didn't. The work was dangerous. Test pilots died—rarely, but inevitably. Bob attended memorials for men he had worked with, analyzed data from accidents that destroyed aircraft and ended lives, confronted the reality that his recommendations could mean the difference between survival and catastrophe.
   375|
   376|### The Fire
   377|
   378|One night early in the morning Bob was working on the experimental RF4C Reconnaissance aircraft in its hangar.  Bob climbed into the cockpit and called to the men working on a wing pylon they gave Bob a thumbs up, so Bob engaged the master power breakers (this is like the key that starts all the systems on the jet. A few seconds later he heard the screaming and saw the pylon under the port wing explode into flames. Bob turned of the power instantly, but it was too late the jet fuel was burning. Bob jumped out of the cockpit onto the starboard wing denting it and climbed to the floor and started running. At that instant it started raining fire suppression foam, it covered everything 3 feet deep. All the tools the books and the crews were covered in foam and so was the open cockpit of the jet. The clean up and the cost was dramatic.  There was a formal safety review board hearing. Eventually Bob was cleared of charges, but he never forgot almost setting a 70 million dollar jet reconnaissance fighter on fire.
   379|
   380|### Heather and Bobby’s Arrival
   381|
   382|*Building a family while the ground shifts beneath you* 
   383|
   384|The babies came, a boy and a girl and as it will the world changed. Nancy gave birth to their daughter and then a son. They named her Heather after English flowers Bob had seen on a business trip. Then came Robert after Bob's father and Grandfather, though they would call him Bobby—a new generation carrying an old name into a new world. The births were not easy. They were both C sections and the second birth had complications that didn’t allow Nancy to have any more children. The second birth came in the middle of the night in a Michigan snowstorm; the hospital was missing a lot of staff and the doctor who delivered was an intern. Bob attended both births and helped the intern and one nurse available in the middle of the night with several other births happening at the same time.  The fact that Nancy couldn’t have more children bothered her for the rest of her life. Heather was a quiet baby, Bobby was a robust baby, hungry and vocal from the first moments, demanding attention.
   385|
   386|Fatherhood was different. At Fermilab, Bob had been able to come home most evenings for dinner, had been present for bedtime routines and weekend activities. The aerospace job demanded more—longer hours, travel to Florida and the UK, emergencies that pulled him away from family at unpredictable times. Nancy bore the burden gracefully, managing two young children, building a life while Bob built his career... She made friends, created a support network that sustained her through Bob's absences. "You chose this," she reminded him, during one argument about a missed birthday party. "You wanted this career. I supported you. But that means you do not get to disappear into it completely. The children need their father, not just your paycheck."She was right, and Bob knew it. He made tried to adjust, set up boundaries, tried to say no to work demands that would take him away from critical family moments. It was a constant negotiation, never balanced, but held in dynamic tension the rest of his career.
   387|
   388|### The 1980s
   389|
   390|Bob had established himself in the Aerospace community, respected for his technical competence. They had built a life in Michigan. They had friends, routines, traditions adapted to their environment—picnics , parades and Nancy’s family. the particular culture of Dutch immigrants. But looking back, he would recognize that time as the end of an era. The last chapter of the life they had chosen before the life they would be forced to live began to unfold.
   391|
   392|### The Dirtiest Job
   393|
   394|Bob had a lot of jobs in his life. Some were prestigious. Some were fun. Some were just plain dirty. The dirtiest job he ever had was also one of the most important. In his job in-charge of engineering and technology he prepared for disaster recovery but in a million years he would never have foreseen the disaster that actually happened. One day after a light rain that bothered no one all the business computers systems just stopped, not crashed, just stopped. The smell quickly pointed to the problem. A bathroom adjacent to the data center had a backed up drain and under the data center elevated floor was a foot, 30cm, of raw sewage covering all the cables and connections connecting dozens of computers and peripherals all shorted out and dead. The cleanup was brutal Bob and his team spent days cleaning connections with Thoth brushes wearing masks and rubber boots. It was the dirtiest job in the history if IT. But in a few days they got everything back online. And that was Bobs dirtiest job. 
   395|
   396|### Chapter xx: Engineer vs. Executive
   397|
   398|*The Evolution of a Career*
   399|
   400|There's a fundamental tension in business between engineers and executives. Engineers want to build the perfect product. Executives want to ship it.
   401|
   402|### A Sick Child
   403|
   404|There's nothing that terrifies a parent more than a sick child. Bob learned this firsthand when my daughter was getting a doctor check up for school sports and the doctor took Bob aside and said “your daughter’s blood counts are dangerously low we need you to get her to a hospital as soon as possible.  They rushed her to the emergency room. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, casting a harsh white glow that made everything look clinical and cold. The doctors ran tests, took blood—more blood than Bob thought shecould possibly have—asked questions about her diet, her activities, her exposures. We sat in the waiting room, waiting, not knowing, watching the clock tick away minutes that felt like hours. Bob had  never felt so helpless. There Bob was, a man who'd worked on complex engineering problems, who'd navigated high-stakes business negotiations, who'd faced down challenges that would have broken lesser men. And he sat in a plastic chair in a hospital corridor, completely and utterly powerless to help his daughter.
   405|
   406|When the doctor finally came out, his face was serious. Not the casual professionalism of routine examinations, but something heavier. Something that communicated, before she even spoke, that what she was about to say would change everything.
   407|
   408|"We've found something," she said. "Your daughter has..."
   409|
   410|Bob doesn't remember what she said after that. He remembers the world going gray, the floor seeming to tilt, the strange sensation of the ground moving.
   411|
   412|Aplastic Anemia. At that time nearly always fatal.
   413|
   414|Nancy and Bob took turns. One of them was always with her, holding our daughter's hand, singing softly to her, reading stories that she was too tired to fully hear. The other took care of our son and tried to keep things normal—making breakfast, driving to school, maintaining the illusion that their. world hadn't been shattered. It always felt Bobs son was missing attention but Bob tried. It was a dark time. The recovery took years and treatments and a hundred blood transfusions but eventually she recovered. She's grown now. She has her own child. She lives a normal life. Bob doesn't take anything for granted in his family. Every birthday is a celebration. Every hug is precious. Every "I love you" is said with the full weight of meaning, because they know—perhaps better than most—how fragile it all can be. The years of terror taught Bob what's important. It taught him to appreciate every moment. It taught him that the things we worry about—the deadlines, the promotions, the arguments about whose turn it is to do the dishes—none of it matters. What matters is the small hand reaching for yours in the darkness.
   415|
   416|### The Engineer
   417|
   418|Bob started as an engineer. He loved the purity of it—the problem-solving, the building, the creation of elegant solutions that worked because they were right, not because someone willed them to work. The best part of being an engineer is when something works. When you've designed something, built it, tested it, and it does exactly what it's supposed to do. There's nothing quite like that feeling. It's a kind of truth. The universe confirms that your understanding is correct, that your creation behaves as you predicted.
   419|
   420|Bob spent his early career in engineering role. Each project was a puzzle. Each solution was a small victory over the chaos of physical reality.
   421|
   422|### The Drive of Fear
   423|
   424|In the wake of such fear, such precious fragility, a strange thing happens in the heart of a parent. You realize that your child is not yours to keep—they are only yours to prepare. And preparation means teaching them to navigate a world that will, eventually, require them to navigate it alone. It means letting go, one small step at a time, trusting that the lessons you've taught and the love you've given will be enough. So when the time came to teach my daughter to drive—to hand over the keys, quite literally, to trust her with a two-ton machine moving at lethal speeds—I understood something that parents who haven't faced the illness of a child might never fully grasp. The fear of losing her had been overwhelming. But the fear of never letting her live—truly live, independently, fully—was somehow greater. Even when she was learning to drive a simple mistake almost killed both Bob and his daughter. A simple slip off the clutch at an intersection and a semi truck cut the bumper off the front of her car. A few more inches and they would have died. But still Bob helped her back on the horse because he knew she needed it.  But he was afraid for her for a long time after.
   425|
   426|### The Executive
   427|
   428|But then Bob became an executive. And he learned a different kind of satisfaction—one that came from entirely different sources. Executive work is about people. It's about making decisions that affect hundreds of employees, their families, their livelihoods. It's about balancing budgets that represent not just numbers but real resources—money that could pay salaries or fund research or keep the lights on. It's about managing stakeholders who have different interests, different priorities, different definitions of success. It's about keeping the company alive long enough to do meaningful work. The satisfaction is different. It's less immediate, more diffuse. You don't get the direct feedback of a working product. You get the feedback of a healthy company—of employees who are engaged, customers who are served, stakeholders who trust you to lead. When Bob first made the transition to executive, he struggled. He missed the directness of engineering, the clear metrics of success, the satisfaction of holding a finished product in my hands. Executive work felt abstract, slippery, impossible to master. But over time, he learned to find satisfaction in different things. A successful negotiation that saved jobs. A restructuring that clarified responsibilities and energized the team. A difficult conversation with an employee that helped them see their potential and grow. These weren't tangible like a working control system, but they were real. They shaped the company, the culture, the people. But there were also the layoffs and downsizing that bit into Bobs soul.
   429|
   430|### What Bob Became 
   431|
   432|Bob tried hard to lead from the front, to respect everyone. It was hard and not always successful. Bob respected both sides—the engineers who want to build the perfect thing, and the executives who need to ship something. Bob created space for both orientations, to translate between the different languages each group speaks. It's not easy. There's always tension. But that's not necessarily bad. Tension creates movement. Movement creates progress.
   433|
   434|###  The Y2K Challenge
   435|
   436|*The Night We Saved the World (Or At Least Our Little Corner of It)*
   437|

   392|
   393|But then Bob became an executive. And he learned a different kind of satisfaction—one that came from entirely different sources. Executive work is about people.    426|### The Symptoms Nobody Named
   427|
   428|Nancy noticed the fatigue first, in the spring—a tiredness that sleep didn't fix, that coffee couldn't touch, that settled into her bones like winter settling into the ground.    429|
   430|### The Waiting Room as Purgatory
   431|
   432|The office smelled of disinfectant and anxiety, a combination Bob would come to associate with the entire medical system.    433|
   434|### The Words That Changed Everything
   435|
   436|Bob would remember the exact geometry of that office for the rest of his life: the desk positioned to give the doctor authority, the chairs arranged to receive bad news, the window behind the desk that looked out on a parking lot where people were going about ordinary lives, unaware that everything was about to change. Bob heard the words, understood their dictionary meanings, but couldn't assemble them into emotional reality. These were terms from medical dramas, from newspaper obituaries, from other people's tragedies. Not from his life. Not from Nancy.
   437|
   438|The meeting continued discussion of referrals, next steps, planning. Bob took notes with the mechanical efficiency that had served him in engineering meetings, recording information his brain could not yet process.    439|
   440|### The First Night
   441|
   442|They didn't tell the children. Not yet. They were living on their own, just starting to find their way.    443|

   445|
   446|### The Machinery of Hope
   447|
   448|The oncology consultations began immediately. Dr. Chen was in his forties, with the brisk competence of someone who had learned to manage grief without being consumed by it. He laid out treatment options with clinical precision: chemotherapy to slow progression, radiation for symptom management, chemotherapy with a possibility of clinical trials that offered long-shot possibilities.
   449|
   450|"Advanced breast cancer is difficult to overcome," she said, not sugarcoating. "But every case is different. Some patients respond better than expected. We'll do everything we can." Everything they could we did, in retrospect it provided a few more years, worth it to Nancy but not a cure. The tumor markers remained stubbornly elevated. The scans showed continued progression into her bones. He found clinical trials, experimental therapies, alternative approaches that ranged from plausible to quackery. Nancy indulged his research initially, but it didn’t yield any relief.  Then the lifetime financial cap on bob’s insurance maxed out, Nancy was stressed by this as they resorted to using retirement savings, but they kept trying, kept living.
   451|
   452|### The Treatment
   453|
   454|The next months were a blur of hospital visits, chemotherapy, and waiting. Waiting for test results. Waiting to see if the treatment was working. Waiting to see if our daughter would live. The chemotherapy of the time was brutal. It killed the cancer cells, yes, but it also killed everything else—her appetite, her energy, her hair, the playful spirit that had once filled our home with laughter. She grew thin and pale, her body a battlefield where war was waged between medicine and disease
   455|
   456|### The New Normal
   457|
   458|They developed routines for the new reality. Nancy's good days and bad days, mapped and managed like weather patterns. The children visiting when they could. Bob reduced his hours at work, delegating responsibilities he would have handled himself six months before. The work that had once consumed him now felt trivial, abstract, distant from the concrete reality of Nancy's diminishing body, the children's grief, the household tasks that multiplied as Nancy's capacity diminished.
   459|
   460|Nancy, despite everything, tried to maintain her life. She continued to work with her nephew (who was a quadriplegic). She kept driving herself to live, she lived to see both children graduate from college and was so proud. Then she achieved her goal she slowly but steadily declined until one day she said I am too tired to go on, take me to the hospital. And that day she passed.
   461|
   462|### The Physiology of Grief
   463|
   464|Bob became, gradually, an expert on dying. Not through study, but through the brutal education of experience over many months. He learned the physical vocabulary of Nancy's decline—the way pain migrated and intensified, the digestive failures that robbed her of nutrition, the edema that swelled her limbs, the jaundice that yellowed her skin as her liver failed. He learned to manage medications, to read the subtle signs that indicated crisis or recovery, to navigate the medical system that treated Nancy as a case while Bob struggled to protect her personhood. Bob struggled to find the right balance, to offer support without taking autonomy, to protect without smothering. It should mean traveling together, growing old together, watching the grandchildren grow up. Not this. Not cleaning up after me when I can't make it to the bathroom." Perhaps it was more love, tested and proven in the crucible of the end.
   465|
   466|### The Morning After
   467|
   468|The immediate aftermath was practical. Phone calls to family, arrangements with the funeral home, the thousand details that death generates. Bob handled them mechanically, grateful for tasks that occupied his mind, that prevented him from sinking into the grief that waited like an ocean beneath a thin crust of ice. The children were bewildered, their grief expressed in separate ways. Felt his own grief expanding to fill every available space.    470|After the children had finally gone to their own homes, Bob sat alone in the living room where he and Nancy had sat many months before, absorbing the news that had destroyed their future. There is a fundamental tension in business between engineers and executives. Engineers want to build the perfect product. Executives want to ship it.
